claim: In 2019, malaria cases were estimated at 229 million, resulting in 409,000 fatal outcomes, primarily in Sub-Saharan Africa as a result of Plasmodium falciparum infection.
source: In 2019, cases were estimated at 229 million, resulting in 409,000 fatal outcomes, primarily in Sub-Saharan Africa as a result of Plasmodium falciparum infection (WHO, 2020).
evidence: Cited from WHO 2020 report

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has compromised malaria treatment and prevention measures.
source: This situation is predicted to worsen as a result of the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic that has compromised malaria treatment and prevention measures (Sherrard-Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Sherrard-Smith et al., 2020

claim: Control and elimination strategies are critically reliant on the continued clinical efficacy of first-line artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) in the absence of an effective licensed malaria vaccine.
source: In the absence of an effective licensed malaria vaccine, control and elimination strategies are critically reliant on the continued clinical efficacy of first-line artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) (White et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from White et al., 2014

claim: ACTs pair fast-acting artemisinin (ART) derivatives with partner drugs such as lumefantrine, amodiaquine, mefloquine, or piperaquine (PPQ).
source: These ACTs pair fast-acting artemisinin (ART) derivatives with partner drugs such as lumefantrine, amodiaquine, mefloquine, or piperaquine (PPQ).
evidence: Direct statement about ACT composition

claim: ART derivatives can reduce the biomass of drug-sensitive parasites by up to 10,000-fold within 48 hr (the duration of one intra-erythrocytic developmental cycle).
source: ART derivatives can reduce the biomass of drug-sensitive parasites by up to 10,000-fold within 48 hr (the duration of one intra-erythrocytic developmental cycle); however, these derivatives are rapidly metabolized in vivo.
evidence: Statement about ART efficacy and metabolism

claim: Longer-lasting, albeit slower-acting, partner drugs are co-administered to reduce the selective pressure for ART resistance and to clear residual parasitemias.
source: Longer-lasting, albeit slower-acting, partner drugs are co-administered to reduce the selective pressure for ART resistance and to clear residual parasitemias (Eastman and Fidock, 2009).
evidence: Cited from Eastman and Fidock, 2009

claim: P. falciparum resistance to ART derivatives has now swept across Southeast (SE) Asia, having first emerged a decade ago in western Cambodia.
source: P. falciparum resistance to ART derivatives has now swept across Southeast (SE) Asia, having first emerged a decade ago in western Cambodia (Dondorp et al., 2009; Noedl et al., 2009; Ariey et al., 2014; Imwong et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources documenting ART resistance emergence

claim: Clinically, ART resistance manifests as delayed clearance of circulating asexual blood stage parasites following treatment with an ACT, but does not result in treatment failure as long as the partner drug remains effective.
source: Clinically, ART resistance manifests as delayed clearance of circulating asexual blood stage parasites following treatment with an ACT, but does not result in treatment failure as long as the partner drug remains effective.
evidence: Statement about clinical manifestation of ART resistance

claim: The accepted threshold for resistance is a parasite clearance half-life of >5.5 hr.
source: The accepted threshold for resistance is a parasite clearance half-life (the time required for the peripheral blood parasite density to decrease by 50%) of >5.5 hr.
evidence: Statement about WHO threshold for resistance

claim: Sensitive parasites are typically cleared in <2–3 hr.
source: Sensitive parasites are typically cleared in <2–3 hr (WHO, 2019).
evidence: Cited from WHO 2019

claim: In vitro, ART resistance manifests as increased survival of tightly synchronized early ring-stage parasites (0–3 hr post invasion) exposed to a 6 hr pulse of 700 nM dihydroartemisinin (DHA) in the ring-stage survival assay (RSA).
source: In vitro, ART resistance manifests as increased survival of tightly synchronized early ring-stage parasites (0–3 hr post invasion) exposed to a 6 hr pulse of 700 nM dihydroartemisinin (DHA, the active metabolite of all ARTs used clinically) in the ring-stage survival assay (RSA) (Witkowski et al., 2013; Ariey et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Witkowski et al., 2013 and Ariey et al., 2014

claim: ART-resistant strains have also acquired resistance to PPQ, which is widely used in SE Asia as a partner drug in combination with DHA.
source: Recently, ART-resistant strains have also acquired resistance to PPQ, which is widely used in SE Asia as a partner drug in combination with DHA (Wicht et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Wicht et al., 2020

claim: Failure rates following DHA-PPQ treatment now exceed 50% in parts of Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam.
source: Failure rates following DHA-PPQ treatment now exceed 50% in parts of Cambodia, Thailand, and Vietnam (van der Pluijm et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from van der Pluijm et al., 2019

claim: ART resistance is primarily determined by mutations in the beta-propeller domain of the P. falciparum Kelch protein K13.
source: In vitro selections, supported by clinical epidemiological data, have demonstrated that ART resistance is primarily determined by mutations in the beta-propeller domain of the P. falciparum Kelch protein K13, also known as Kelch13 (Ariey et al., 2014; Ashley et al., 2014; MalariaGEN Plasmodium falciparum Community Project, 2016; Ménard et al., 2016; Siddiqui et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources documenting K13 mutations and resistance

claim: K13 mutations result in reduced endocytosis of host-derived hemoglobin and thereby decrease the release of Fe2+-heme that serves to activate ART, thus reducing the drug's potency.
source: Recent evidence suggests that these mutations result in reduced endocytosis of host-derived hemoglobin and thereby decrease the release of Fe2+-heme that serves to activate ART, thus reducing the drug's potency (Yang et al., 2019; Birnbaum et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Yang et al., 2019 and Birnbaum et al., 2020

claim: Mutations in ferredoxin (fd) and multidrug resistance protein 2 (mdr2) have been associated with ART resistance in K13 mutant parasites.
source: Mutations in other genes including ferredoxin (fd) and multidrug resistance protein 2 (mdr2) have also been associated with ART resistance in K13 mutant parasites, leading to the suggestion that they may contribute to a multigenic basis of resistance and/or parasite fitness, or serve as genetic markers of founder populations (Miotto et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Miotto et al., 2015

claim: In SE Asia, the most prevalent K13 mutation is C580Y, which associates with delayed clearance in vivo.
source: In SE Asia, the most prevalent K13 mutation is C580Y, which associates with delayed clearance in vivo (Ariey et al., 2014; Ashley et al., 2014; MalariaGEN Plasmodium falciparum Community Project, 2016; Ménard et al., 2016; Imwong et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources documenting C580Y prevalence and association with delayed clearance

claim: The C580Y mutation mediates ART resistance in vitro, as demonstrated by RSAs performed on gene-edited parasites.
source: This mutation also mediates ART resistance in vitro, as demonstrated by RSAs performed on gene-edited parasites (Ghorbal et al., 2014; Straimer et al., 2015; Straimer et al., 2017; Mathieu et al., 2020; Uwimana et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from multiple gene editing studies

claim: Nearly 200 other K13 mutations have been documented in SE Asia and other malaria-endemic regions, including the Guiana Shield and the western Pacific.
source: Other studies have documented the emergence of nearly 200 other K13 mutations, both in SE Asia and in other malaria-endemic regions, including the Guiana Shield and the western Pacific (MalariaGEN Plasmodium falciparum Community Project, 2016; Ménard et al., 2016; Das et al., 2019; WWARN K13 Genotype-Phenotype Study Group, 2019; Mathieu et al., 2020; Miotto et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from multiple surveillance studies

claim: Only a handful of K13 mutations (N458Y, M476I, Y493H, R539T, I543T, and R561H) have been validated by gene-editing experiments as conferring ART resistance in vitro aside from C580Y.
source: Aside from C580Y, however, only a handful of other K13 mutations (N458Y, M476I, Y493H, R539T, I543T, and R561H) have been validated by gene-editing experiments as conferring ART resistance in vitro (Straimer et al., 2015; Siddiqui et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Straimer et al., 2015 and Siddiqui et al., 2020

claim: Multiple mutations in K13 have been associated with the clinical delayed clearance phenotype and have been proposed as candidate markers of ART resistance.
source: Nonetheless, multiple mutations in this gene have been associated with the clinical delayed clearance phenotype and have been proposed as candidate markers of ART resistance (WWARN K13 Genotype-Phenotype Study Group, 2019; WHO, 2019).
evidence: Cited from WWARN K13 Genotype-Phenotype Study Group, 2019 and WHO, 2019

claim: The K13 R561H mutation was first associated with delayed parasite clearance in SE Asia.
source: We include the K13 R561H mutation, first associated with delayed parasite clearance in SE Asia (Ashley et al., 2014; Phyo et al., 2016), and very recently identified at up to 13% prevalence in certain districts in Rwanda (Uwimana et al., 2020; Bergmann et al., 2021; Uwimana et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Ashley et al., 2014 and Phyo et al., 2016

claim: The K13 R561H mutation has been identified at up to 13% prevalence in certain districts in Rwanda.
source: We include the K13 R561H mutation, first associated with delayed parasite clearance in SE Asia (Ashley et al., 2014; Phyo et al., 2016), and very recently identified at up to 13% prevalence in certain districts in Rwanda (Uwimana et al., 2020; Bergmann et al., 2021; Uwimana et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Uwimana et al., 2020, Bergmann et al., 2021, and Uwimana et al., 2021

claim: K13 mutations can impart ART resistance across multiple Asian and African strains, at levels that vary widely depending on the mutation and the parasite genetic background.
source: Our results show that K13 mutations can impart ART resistance across multiple Asian and African strains, at levels that vary widely depending on the mutation and the parasite genetic background.
evidence: Summary statement of study results

claim: Compared with K13 mutant Asian parasites, stronger in vitro fitness costs were observed in most K13 edited African strains.
source: Compared with K13 mutant Asian parasites, we observed stronger in vitro fitness costs in most K13 edited African strains, which might predict a slower dissemination of ART resistance in high-transmission African settings.
evidence: Summary statement of study results

claim: The R561H mutation confers elevated RSA survival and a minimal fitness cost in African 3D7 parasites.
source: Nonetheless, our data highlight the threat of the R561H mutation emerging in Rwanda, which confers elevated RSA survival and a minimal fitness cost in African 3D7 parasites.
evidence: Summary statement of study results

claim: 98% (3179) of all African samples analyzed were K13 wild-type.
source: Of all samples, 98% (3179) were K13 wild-type, that is, they matched the 3D7 (African) reference sequence or harbored a synonymous (non-coding) mutation.
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping of African samples

claim: For individual African countries, the percentage of K13 wild-type samples ranged from 95% to 100%.
source: For individual countries, the percentage of K13 wild-type samples ranged from 95% to 100% (Figure 1; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping shown in Figure 1

claim: 35 unique non-synonymous mutations in K13 were identified in African samples.
source: In total, we identified 35 unique non-synonymous mutations in K13.
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping of African samples

claim: Only two K13 mutations have been validated as resistance mediators in the SE Asian Dd2 strain: M476I and R561H.
source: Of these, only two have been validated as resistance mediators in the SE Asian Dd2 strain: the M476I mutation initially identified from long-term ART selection studies, and the R561H mutation observed in SE Asia and now in Rwanda (Ariey et al., 2014; Straimer et al., 2015; Uwimana et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Ariey et al., 2014, Straimer et al., 2015, and Uwimana et al., 2020

claim: Of the 35 non-synonymous mutations in African samples, only two were present in ≥10 samples: R561H (n=20) and A578S (n=10).
source: Of the 35 non-synonymous mutations, only two were present in ≥ten samples: R561H (n=20, found only in Rwanda, sampled from 2012 to 2015; Uwimana et al., 2020), and A578S (n=10; observed in four African countries across multiple years).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping of African samples

claim: A578S was shown not to confer in vitro resistance in Dd2.
source: Previously, A578S was shown not to confer in vitro resistance in Dd2 (Ménard et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Ménard et al., 2016

claim: In the set of 927 genotyped Rwandan isolates, R561H accounted for 44% of mutant samples and 2% of all samples.
source: In the set of 927 genotyped Rwandan isolates, R561H accounted for 44% of mutant samples and 2% of all samples (Figure 1 inset).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping of Rwandan samples shown in Figure 1

claim: 3D7 segregates phylogenetically with parasites from Rwanda based on whole-genome sequence analysis of African isolates.
source: On the basis of whole-genome sequence analysis of African isolates, 3D7 was recently shown to segregate phylogenetically with parasites from Rwanda (Uwimana et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Uwimana et al., 2020

claim: F32 was derived from an isolate from Tanzania.
source: F32 was derived from an isolate from Tanzania (Witkowski et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from Witkowski et al., 2010

claim: For 3D7 parasites, the highest RSA survival rates were observed with 3D7R561H parasites, which averaged 6.6% RSA survival.
source: For 3D7 parasites, the highest RSA survival rates were observed with 3D7R561H parasites, which averaged 6.6% RSA survival.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 2A

claim: For the 3D7M579I and 3D7C580Y lines, mean RSA survival rates were both 4.8%, a three- to fourfold increase relative to the 3D7WT line.
source: For the 3D7M579I and 3D7C580Y lines, mean RSA survival rates were both 4.8%, a three- to fourfold increase relative to the 3D7WT line.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 2A

claim: No elevated RSA survival was seen in a 3D7 control line (3D7ctrl) that expresses only the silent shield mutations used at the guide RNA (gRNA) cut site.
source: No elevated RSA survival was seen in a 3D7 control line (3D7ctrl) that expresses only the silent shield mutations used at the guide RNA (gRNA) cut site (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 2A

claim: Western blots revealed an ~30% reduction in K13 protein expression levels in 3D7R561H, 3D7M579I, and 3D7C580Y lines relative to the parental 3D7WT line.
source: Western blots performed on tightly synchronized ring-stage parasites revealed an ~30% reduction in K13 protein expression levels in these three K13 mutant lines relative to the parental 3D7WT line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Data from Western blot experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: For F32 parasites, the introduction of K13 mutations yielded no significant increases in RSA survival, with survival rates in the range of 0.3% to 0.5% for lines expressing R561H, M579I, C580Y, or wild-type K13.
source: Interestingly, for F32 parasites, the introduction of K13 mutations yielded no significant increases in RSA survival, with survival rates in the range of 0.3% to 0.5% for lines expressing R561H, M579I, C580Y, or wild-type K13. (Figure 2B).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 2B

claim: Introduction of M476I into F32 parasites resulted in a modest gain of resistance (mean survival of 1.7%), while this same mutation conferred RSA survival levels of ~10% in edited Dd2 parasites.
source: Previously we reported that introduction of M476I into F32 parasites resulted in a modest gain of resistance (mean survival of 1.7%), while this same mutation conferred RSA survival levels of ~10% in edited Dd2 parasites (Straimer et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Straimer et al., 2015

claim: Editing of M579I and C580Y into UG659 yielded moderate RSA survival rates (means of 6.3% and 4.7% for UG659M579I or UG659C580Y respectively, vs 1.0% for UG659WT).
source: Editing of both mutations into UG659 yielded moderate RSA survival rates (means of 6.3% and 4.7% for UG659M579I or UG659C580Y respectively, vs 1.0% for UG659WT; Figure 2C).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 2C

claim: Introducing K13 M579I or C580Y into UG815 yielded the highest rates of in vitro resistance, with mean survival levels reaching ~12% in both UG815M579I and UG815C580Y.
source: Strikingly, introducing K13 M579I or C580Y into UG815 yielded the highest rates of in vitro resistance, with mean survival levels reaching ~12% in both UG815M579I and UG815C580Y.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 2D

claim: M579I and C580Y conferred equivalent levels of resistance in edited Dd2 parasites (RSA survival rates of 4.0% and 4.7%, respectively).
source: M579I and C580Y also conferred equivalent levels of resistance in edited Dd2 parasites (RSA survival rates of 4.0% and 4.7%, respectively; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments

claim: The K13 M579I and C580Y mutations each conferred significant fitness defects in most strains tested, with the proportions of K13 mutant lines declining over time.
source: Results showed that the K13 M579I and C580Y mutations each conferred significant fitness defects in most strains tested, with the proportions of K13 mutant lines declining over time.
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 3

claim: For M579I and C580Y mutations, the largest reductions in fitness were observed with edited 3D7 or UG815 parasites.
source: For both mutations, the largest reductions were observed with edited 3D7 or UG815 parasites.
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 3

claim: M579I and C580Y mutations exerted a minimal impact on fitness in UG659.
source: In contrast, these mutations exerted a minimal impact on fitness in UG659.
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 3C

claim: R561H had no impact on fitness in 3D7 parasites.
source: For R561H, we observed no impact on fitness in 3D7 parasites, although in F32 this mutation exerted a fitness defect similar to M579I and C580Y (Figure 3A–D; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 3A

claim: In F32, R561H exerted a fitness defect similar to M579I and C580Y.
source: For R561H, we observed no impact on fitness in 3D7 parasites, although in F32 this mutation exerted a fitness defect similar to M579I and C580Y (Figure 3A–D; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 3B

claim: Fitness costs ranged from <1% to 12% per generation across mutations and lines, with the lowest costs observed in 3D7R561H and UG659C580Y parasites, and the greatest costs observed in the K13 edited UG815 lines.
source: These costs ranged from <1% to 12% per generation across mutations and lines, with the lowest costs observed in 3D7R561H and UG659C580Y parasites, and the greatest costs observed in the K13 edited UG815 lines (Figure 3E).
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 3E

claim: High RSA survival rates were generally accompanied by high fitness costs, and conversely low fitness costs were associated with low survival rates, with exceptions being the 3D7R561H and UG659C580Y lines.
source: Comparing data across these four African strains revealed that high RSA survival rates were generally accompanied by high fitness costs, and conversely that low fitness costs were associated with low survival rates. Exceptions were the 3D7R561H and UG659C580Y lines that showed moderate resistance with little to no apparent fitness costs (Figure 3F).
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 3F

claim: 19 nonsynonymous polymorphisms in K13 were identified across all regions and years in Cambodia.
source: In sum, 19 nonsynonymous polymorphisms in K13 were identified across all regions and years.
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping of Cambodian samples

claim: Of the 19 K13 mutations in Cambodia, only three were present in >10 samples: Y493H (n=83), R539T (n=87), and C580Y (n=1915).
source: Of these, only three were present in >10 samples: Y493H (n=83), R539T (n=87), and C580Y (n=1915).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping of Cambodian samples

claim: Y493H, R539T, and C580Y mutations were previously shown to confer ART resistance in vitro.
source: Each of these mutations was previously shown to confer ART resistance in vitro (Straimer et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Straimer et al., 2015

claim: In northern and eastern Cambodia, 96% of isolates in 2001–2002 were K13 wild type.
source: This analysis revealed a significant proportion of K13 wild-type parasites in the early 2000s, particularly in northern and eastern Cambodia, where 96% of isolates in 2001–2002 were wild type (Figure 4).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping shown in Figure 4

claim: In western Cambodia, the wild-type allele percentage in 2001–2002 had already fallen to 56%.
source: In western Cambodia, where ART resistance first emerged (Dondorp et al., 2009; Noedl et al., 2009), the wild-type allele percentage in 2001–2002 had already fallen to 56%.
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping shown in Figure 4A

claim: Delayed parasite clearance following ACT or artesunate treatment was first documented in 2008–2009.
source: This is striking given that delayed parasite clearance following ACT or artesunate treatment was first documented in 2008–2009 (Noedl et al., 2008; Noedl et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Noedl et al., 2008 and Noedl et al., 2009

claim: In all four regions of Cambodia, the frequency of the wild-type allele declined substantially over time and the diversity of mutant alleles contracted, with nearly all wild-type and non-K13 C580Y mutant parasites being replaced by parasites harboring the C580Y mutation.
source: In all four regions, the frequency of the wild-type allele declined substantially over time and the diversity of mutant alleles contracted, with nearly all wild-type and non-K13 C580Y mutant parasites being replaced by parasites harboring the C580Y mutation (Figure 4).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping shown in Figure 4

claim: In western and southern Cambodia, the prevalence of C580Y in 2016–2017 effectively attained 100%, increasing from 22% and 58% in the initial sample sets, respectively.
source: This effect was particularly pronounced in the western and the southern regions, where the prevalence of C580Y in 2016–2017 effectively attained 100%, increasing from 22% and 58% in the initial sample sets, respectively (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping shown in Figure 4A and 4D

claim: In northern and eastern Cambodia, C580Y also outcompeted all other mutant alleles; however, 19–25% of parasites remained K13 wild type in 2016–2017.
source: In northern and eastern Cambodia, C580Y also outcompeted all other mutant alleles; however, 19–25% of parasites remained K13 wild type in 2016–2017 (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping shown in Figure 4B and 4C

claim: F446I is the predominant K13 mutation in Myanmar.
source: F446I is the predominant mutation in Myanmar (Imwong et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Imwong et al., 2020

claim: P553L, R561H, and P574L have each been shown to have multiple independent origins throughout SE Asia.
source: P553L, R561H, and P574L have each been shown to have multiple independent origins throughout SE Asia (Ménard et al., 2016) and were identified at low frequencies in our sequencing study in Cambodia (Figure 4).
evidence: Cited from Ménard et al., 2016

claim: The E252Q mutation was formerly prevalent on the Thai-Myanmar border, and has been associated with delayed parasite clearance in vivo despite its location upstream of the beta-propeller domain.
source: Lastly, the E252Q mutation was formerly prevalent on the Thai-Myanmar border, and, despite its location upstream of the beta-propeller domain, has been associated with delayed parasite clearance in vivo (Anderson et al., 2017; Cerqueira et al., 2017; WWARN K13 Genotype-Phenotype Study Group, 2019).
evidence: Cited from Anderson et al., 2017, Cerqueira et al., 2017, and WWARN K13 Genotype-Phenotype Study Group, 2019

claim: Both the P553L and R561H mutations yielded mean RSA survival rates comparable to C580Y (4.6% or 4.3% RSA survival for Dd2P553L or Dd2R561H, respectively, vs 4.7% for Dd2C580Y).
source: Both the P553L and R561H mutations yielded mean RSA survival rates comparable to C580Y (4.6% or 4.3% RSA survival for Dd2P553L or Dd2R561H, respectively, vs 4.7% for Dd2C580Y; Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 5A

claim: F446I and P574L showed only modest increases in survival relative to the wild-type parental line (2.0% and 2.1% for Dd2F446I and Dd2P574L, respectively, vs 0.6% for Dd2WT).
source: F446I and P574L showed only modest increases in survival relative to the wild-type parental line (2.0% and 2.1% for Dd2F446I and Dd2P574L, respectively, vs 0.6% for Dd2WT).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 5A

claim: No change in RSA survival relative to Dd2WT was observed for the Dd2E252Q line.
source: No change in RSA survival relative to Dd2WT was observed for the Dd2E252Q line.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 5A

claim: The resistant benchmark Dd2R539T showed a mean RSA survival level of 20.0%.
source: The resistant benchmark Dd2R539T showed a mean RSA survival level of 20.0%, consistent with earlier reports of this mutation conferring high-grade ART resistance in vitro (Straimer et al., 2015; Straimer et al., 2017).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 5A

claim: Editing of the F446I, P553L, and P574L mutations into Cambodian Cam3.IIWT parasites did not result in statistically significant increases in survival rates relative to the K13 wild-type line.
source: In contrast to Dd2, editing of the F446I, P553L, and P574L mutations into Cambodian Cam3.IIWT parasites did not result in statistically significant increases in survival rates relative to the K13 wild-type line, in part because the background survival rate of Cam3.IIWT was higher than for Dd2WT.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 5B

claim: The E252Q mutation did not result in elevated RSA survival in the Cam3.II background.
source: The E252Q mutation did not result in elevated RSA survival in the Cam3.II background, a result also observed with Dd2.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 5B

claim: ART resistance was apparent upon introduction of the R561H mutation into Cam3.IIWT parasites, with mean survival rates for Cam3.IIR561H exceeding those for the Cam3.IIC580Y line (13.2% vs 10.0%, respectively).
source: Nonetheless, ART resistance was apparent upon introduction of the R561H mutation into Cam3.IIWT parasites, with mean survival rates for Cam3.IIR561H exceeding those for the Cam3.IIC580Y line (13.2% vs 10.0%, respectively).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 5B

claim: The F446I, P553L, and C580Y mutations resulted in minimal growth impact in Dd2 parasites.
source: These data provided evidence of a minimal growth impact with the F446I, P553L, and C580Y mutations.
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 5C

claim: E252Q, R561H, and P574L resulted in greater fitness costs when compared to Dd2WT parasites.
source: In contrast, E252Q, R561H, and P574L resulted in greater fitness costs when compared to Dd2WT parasites (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 5C

claim: Both the C580Y and P553L mutations yielded elevated RSA survival and minimal fitness costs in the Dd2 strain, providing optimal traits for dissemination.
source: Both the C580Y and P553L mutations yielded elevated RSA survival and minimal fitness costs in the Dd2 strain, providing optimal traits for dissemination (Figure 5D).
evidence: Data from RSA and fitness assays shown in Figure 5D

claim: All fitness costs in K13 edited Dd2 parasites were considerably lower than those observed in the majority of the K13 edited African lines.
source: We note that all fitness costs in K13 edited Dd2 parasites were considerably lower than those observed in the majority of the K13 edited African lines described above (Figure 3).
evidence: Comparison of fitness data between Dd2 and African lines

claim: The C580Y mutation yielded mean survival rates ranging from 2.1% to 15.4% in edited Thai parasites, demonstrating a major contribution of the parasite genetic background in dictating the level of mutant K13-mediated ART resistance.
source: These studies revealed a major contribution of the parasite genetic background in dictating the level of mutant K13-mediated ART resistance, as exemplified by the C580Y mutation, which yielded mean survival rates ranging from 2.1% to 15.4% in edited parasites.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 6

claim: The R561H mutation consistently yielded moderate to high in vitro resistance, at or above the level of C580Y in Thai isolates.
source: Trends observed for individual mutations were maintained across strains, with the R561H mutation consistently yielding moderate to high in vitro resistance, at or above the level of C580Y.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 6

claim: E252Q edited parasites did not display significant increases in survival rates relative to isogenic K13 wild-type lines in Thai isolates.
source: Consistent with our Dd2 results, E252Q edited parasites did not display significant increases in survival rates relative to isogenic K13 wild-type lines (Figure 6A–E; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 6A-E

claim: Two unedited culture-adapted Thai isolates (Thai6E252Q and Thai7E252Q) expressing the K13 E252Q mutation exhibited mean RSA survival rates above the 1% threshold for ART sensitivity (2.7% for Thai6E252Q and 5.1% for Thai7E252Q).
source: We also profiled two unedited culture-adapted Thai isolates (Thai6E252Q and Thai7E252Q), which express the K13 E252Q mutation that occurs upstream of the propeller domain. Notably, both lines exhibited mean RSA survival rates above the 1% threshold for ART sensitivity (2.7% for Thai6E252Q and 5.1% for Thai7E252Q; Figure 6F).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 6F

claim: Additional genetic factors present in Thai6E252Q and Thai7E252Q isolates are required for E252Q to manifest ART resistance.
source: These data suggest that additional genetic factors present in these two Thai isolates are required for E252Q to manifest ART resistance.
evidence: Inference from RSA data on Thai isolates

claim: In a prior genome-wide association study of SE Asian parasites, K13-mediated ART resistance was associated with the D193Y and T484I mutations in the ferredoxin (fd) and multidrug resistance protein 2 (mdr2) genes, respectively.
source: In a prior genome-wide association study of SE Asian parasites, K13-mediated ART resistance was associated with the D193Y and T484I mutations in the ferredoxin (fd) and multidrug resistance protein 2 (mdr2) genes, respectively (Miotto et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Miotto et al., 2015

claim: Isogenic RF7C580Y parasites expressing either the mutant or wild-type fd residue at position 193 showed no difference in RSA survival rates, either at 700 nM or across a range of DHA concentrations down to 1.4 nM.
source: Isogenic RF7C580Y parasites expressing either the mutant or wild-type fd residue at position 193 showed no difference in RSA survival rates, either at 700 nM (averaging ~27%), or across a range of DHA concentrations down to 1.4 nM (Figure 7A,C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 7A and 7C

claim: Editing fd D193Y into the recombinant CamWTC580Y line that expresses K13 C580Y had no impact on RSA survival (mean RSA survival rate of 11% vs 12.5%).
source: Editing fd D193Y into the recombinant CamWTC580Y line that expresses K13 C580Y (Straimer et al., 2015) also had no impact on RSA survival (mean RSA survival rate of 11% vs 12.5%).
evidence: Data from RSA experiments

claim: Cam3.IIC580Y parasites maintained the same rates of in vitro RSA survival (means ~19–22%) irrespective of their mdr2 allele.
source: Likewise, Cam3.IIC580Y parasites maintained the same rates of in vitro RSA survival (means ~19–22%) irrespective of their mdr2 allele.
evidence: Data from RSA experiments shown in Figure 7C

claim: eGFP-based fitness assays revealed no changes in growth rates for fd or mdr2 edited RF7C580Y or Cam3.IIC580Y lines compared with their wild-type controls.
source: eGFP-based fitness assays initiated at different starting ratios of the Dd2 eGFP+ reporter line and fd or mdr2 edited RF7C580Y or Cam3.IIC580Y lines revealed no changes in growth rates for mutant lines compared with their wild-type controls (Figure 7B,D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 7B and 7D

claim: The fd D193Y and mdr2 T484I mutations may be markers of ART-resistant founder populations, but themselves do not contribute directly to ART resistance or augment parasite fitness.
source: These data suggest that the fd D193Y and mdr2 T484I mutations may be markers of ART-resistant founder populations, but themselves do not contribute directly to ART resistance or augment parasite fitness.
evidence: Inference from RSA and fitness data on fd and mdr2 edited lines

claim: Certain African strains present no major biological obstacle to becoming ART resistant in vitro upon acquiring K13 mutations.
source: Collectively, our results provide evidence that certain African strains present no major biological obstacle to becoming ART resistant in vitro upon acquiring K13 mutations.
evidence: Summary statement based on RSA data from African strains

claim: K13 C580Y may not easily take hold in Africa where infections are often highly polyclonal, generating intra-host competition that impacts a strain's ability to succeed at the population level.
source: These data suggest that K13 C580Y may not easily take hold in Africa where, unlike in SE Asia, infections are often highly polyclonal, generating intra-host competition that impacts a strain's ability to succeed at the population level.
evidence: Speculation based on fitness data and knowledge of African malaria epidemiology

claim: Individuals in highly-endemic African settings generally have high levels of acquired immunity, potentially minimizing infection by relatively unfit parasites.
source: In addition, individuals in highly-endemic African settings generally have high levels of acquired immunity, potentially minimizing infection by relatively unfit parasites, and often have asymptomatic infections that go untreated and are thus less subject to selective drug pressure compared with individuals in SE Asia (Eastman and Fidock, 2009).
evidence: Cited from Eastman and Fidock, 2009

claim: Fitness costs caused by mutations in PfCRT resulted in the rapid resurgence of wild-type parasites following the implementation of other first-line antimalarial therapies in Africa after chloroquine use.
source: This situation recalls the history of chloroquine use in Africa, where fitness costs caused by mutations in the primary resistance determinant PfCRT resulted in the rapid resurgence of wild-type parasites following the implementation of other first-line antimalarial therapies (Kublin et al., 2003; Laufer et al., 2006; Ord et al., 2007; Frosch et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from multiple sources documenting chloroquine resistance history

claim: The M579I mutation was earlier detected in an infection acquired in Equatorial Guinea with evidence of in vivo ART resistance, but was notably absent in all 3257 African samples reported in this study.
source: An even greater fitness cost was observed with the M579I mutation, earlier detected in an infection acquired in Equatorial Guinea with evidence of in vivo ART resistance (Lu et al., 2017), but which was notably absent in all 3257 African samples reported herein.
evidence: Cited from Lu et al., 2017 and data from this study

claim: Samples collected by others in Rwanda in 2018 and 2019 identified the R561H mutation at 12–13% prevalence.
source: While our Rwandan samples from 2012 to 2015 observed this mutation at 2% prevalence, samples collected by others in 2018 and 2019 identified this mutation at 12–13% prevalence (Bergmann et al., 2021; Uwimana et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Bergmann et al., 2021 and Uwimana et al., 2021

claim: One report included evidence associating R561H with delayed parasite clearance in patients treated with the ACT artemether-lumefantrine.
source: One of these reports included evidence associating R561H with delayed parasite clearance in patients treated with the ACT artemether-lumefantrine (Uwimana et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Uwimana et al., 2021

claim: The C580Y mutation was already at high prevalence in western Cambodia several years before the first published reports of delayed parasite clearance in ART-treated patients.
source: Interestingly, this mutation was already at high prevalence in western Cambodia several years before the first published reports of delayed parasite clearance in ART-treated patients (Noedl et al., 2008; Dondorp et al., 2009; Ariey et al., 2014).
evidence: Data from K13 genotyping and cited reports

claim: The success of C580Y in Cambodia cannot be explained by resistance alone, as R539T and I543T variants conferred greater ART resistance in vitro.
source: The success of this mutation in Cambodia, and elsewhere in the eastern Greater Mekong subregion (Imwong et al., 2020), cannot be explained by resistance alone, as we previously reported that the less common R539T and I543T variants conferred greater ART resistance in vitro (Straimer et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Imwong et al., 2020 and Straimer et al., 2015

claim: F446I has spread across Myanmar despite conferring low-level resistance.
source: Similarly, we now report that the R561H and P553L mutations yield ART resistance at levels comparable to C580Y in Dd2 parasites. In contrast, low-level resistance was observed with F446I, which has nonetheless spread across Myanmar (Imwong et al., 2020).
evidence: Data from this study and cited from Imwong et al., 2020

claim: In a separate recent gene editing study, F446I yielded no significant in vitro resistance in 3D7 parasites and was fitness neutral.
source: In a separate recent gene editing study, F446I yielded no significant in vitro resistance in 3D7 parasites and was fitness neutral (Siddiqui et al., 2020), consistent with our findings for this mutation in edited Dd2 parasites.
evidence: Cited from Siddiqui et al., 2020

claim: The C580Y mutation generally exerts less of a fitness cost relative to other K13 variants in Asian Dd2 parasites.
source: Our studies into the impact of K13 mutations on in vitro growth in Asian Dd2 parasites provide evidence that the C580Y mutation generally exerts less of a fitness cost relative to other K13 variants, as measured in K13 edited parasites co-cultured with an eGFP+ reporter line.
evidence: Data from fitness assays shown in Figure 5

claim: P553L was similarly fitness neutral compared with C580Y and showed similar RSA values in Dd2 parasites.
source: A notable exception was P553L, which compared with C580Y was similarly fitness neutral and showed similar RSA values.
evidence: Data from fitness and RSA assays shown in Figure 5

claim: P553L has proven far less successful in its regional dissemination compared with C580Y despite similar fitness and resistance profiles.
source: P553L has nonetheless proven far less successful in its regional dissemination compared with C580Y (Ménard et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from Ménard et al., 2016

claim: Additional factors have contributed to the success of C580Y in sweeping across SE Asia, possibly including specific genetic backgrounds that have favored the dissemination of C580Y parasites or ACT use that favored the selection of partner drug resistance.
source: These data suggest that additional factors have contributed to the success of C580Y in sweeping across SE Asia. These might include specific genetic backgrounds that have favored the dissemination of C580Y parasites, possibly resulting in enhanced transmission potential (Witmer et al., 2020), or ACT use that favored the selection of partner drug resistance in these parasite backgrounds (van der Pluijm et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation based on data and cited sources

claim: The most detrimental impacts on growth rates in isogenic Dd2 lines were observed with E252Q and R561H, which earlier predominated near the Thailand-Myanmar border region, but were later overtaken by C580Y.
source: In terms of growth rates in our isogenic Dd2 lines, the most detrimental impacts were observed with E252Q and R561H, which earlier predominated near the Thailand-Myanmar border region, but were later overtaken by C580Y (Phyo et al., 2016).
evidence: Data from fitness assays and cited from Phyo et al., 2016

claim: C580Y produced an optimal combination of no measurable fitness cost and relatively high RSA survival rates in Dd2 parasites.
source: In our study, C580Y produced an optimal combination of no measurable fitness cost and relatively high RSA survival rates in Dd2 parasites.
evidence: Data from fitness and RSA assays

claim: In a prior independent study, R561H showed slightly improved fitness relative to C580Y in paired isogenic parasites from Thailand (generated in the NHP4302 strain).
source: In a prior independent study, however, R561H showed slightly improved fitness relative to C580Y in paired isogenic parasites from Thailand (generated in the NHP4302 strain), providing further evidence that both fitness and resistance are strain-dependent (Nair et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Nair et al., 2018

claim: Proposed candidates for secondary genetic determinants that could augment mutant K13-mediated ART resistance have included fd, mdr2, ap-2μ, ubp1, and pfcoronin.
source: Further research is required to define secondary genetic determinants that could augment mutant K13-mediated ART resistance, and to explore other potential mediators of resistance. Proposed candidates have included fd, mdr2, ap-2μ, ubp1, and pfcoronin, which have earlier been associated with P. falciparum ART susceptibility (Demas et al., 2018; Henrici et al., 2019; Sutherland et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Demas et al., 2018, Henrici et al., 2019, and Sutherland et al., 2021

claim: No evident association was observed between the genotypes of pfcrt, mdr1, arps10, ap-2μ, or ubp1 and the degree to which mutant K13 conferred ART resistance in vitro in the set of African or Asian strains tested.
source: We also observed no evident association between the genotypes of pfcrt, mdr1, arps10, ap-2μ, or ubp1 and the degree to which mutant K13 conferred ART resistance in vitro in our set of African or Asian strains (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Data from genotyping and RSA experiments

claim: Mutations associated with enhanced DNA repair mechanisms have been observed in ART-resistant SE Asian parasites, supporting the idea that mutant K13 parasites may have an improved ability to repair ART-mediated DNA damage.
source: Mutations associated with enhanced DNA repair mechanisms have also been observed in ART-resistant SE Asian parasites, supporting the idea that mutant K13 parasites may have an improved ability to repair ART-mediated DNA damage (Xiong et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Xiong et al., 2020

claim: P. falciparum genomic structures in Africa tend to be far more diverse than in the epicenter of resistance in Cambodia, where parasite strains are highly sub-structured into a few lineages that can readily maintain complex genetic traits.
source: At the population level, we note that P. falciparum genomic structures in Africa tend to be far more diverse than in the epicenter of resistance in Cambodia, where parasite strains are highly sub-structured into a few lineages that can readily maintain complex genetic traits (Amato et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Amato et al., 2018

claim: A requirement to transmit mutant K13 and additional determinants of resistance in African malaria-endemic settings, where genetic outcrossing is the norm, would predict that ART resistance will spread more gradually on this continent than in SE Asia.
source: A requirement to transmit mutant K13 and additional determinants of resistance in African malaria-endemic settings, where genetic outcrossing is the norm, would predict that ART resistance will spread more gradually on this continent than in SE Asia.
evidence: Speculation based on knowledge of parasite genetics and transmission

claim: Identifying secondary determinants that allow African strains to offset fitness costs associated with mutant K13 could be possible using genome-wide association studies or genetic crosses between ART-resistant and sensitive African parasites in the human liver-chimeric mouse model of P. falciparum infection.
source: It is nonetheless possible that secondary determinants will allow some African strains to offset fitness costs associated with mutant K13, or otherwise augment K13-mediated ART resistance. Identifying such determinants could be possible using genome-wide association studies or genetic crosses between ART-resistant and sensitive African parasites in the human liver-chimeric mouse model of P. falciparum infection (Vaughan et al., 2015; Amambua-Ngwa et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Vaughan et al., 2015 and Amambua-Ngwa et al., 2019

claim: Reduced transmission rates in areas of Africa where malaria is declining, leading to lower levels of immunity, may also benefit the emergence and dissemination of mutant K13.
source: Reduced transmission rates in areas of Africa where malaria is declining, leading to lower levels of immunity, may also benefit the emergence and dissemination of mutant K13 (Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019).
evidence: Cited from Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019

claim: The continued potent activity of lumefantrine, the partner drug in the first line treatment artemether-lumefantrine, is an impediment to the dissemination of ART resistance in Africa.
source: Another impediment to the dissemination of ART resistance in Africa is the continued potent activity of lumefantrine, the partner drug in the first line treatment artemether-lumefantrine (Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019).
evidence: Cited from Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019

claim: In SE Asia, ART-resistant parasites have also developed high-level resistance to the partner drug PPQ, with widespread treatment failures enabling the dissemination of multidrug-resistant strains.
source: This situation contrasts with SE Asia where ART-resistant parasites have also developed high-level resistance to the partner drug PPQ, with widespread treatment failures enabling the dissemination of multidrug-resistant strains (Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019; van der Pluijm et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Conrad and Rosenthal, 2019 and van der Pluijm et al., 2019

claim: Recent molecular surveillance studies reveal a low prevalence of mutant K13 in Africa.
source: While the genotyping data presented herein and other recent molecular surveillance studies reveal a low prevalence of mutant K13 in Africa (Kayiba et al., 2021; Schmedes et al., 2021), the emergence and spread of the R561H variant in Rwanda is cause for significant concern.
evidence: Data from this study and cited from Kayiba et al., 2021 and Schmedes et al., 2021

claim: The emergence of R561H in Rwanda is a harbinger of subsequent partner drug resistance and ACT treatment failure.
source: These data call for continuous continent-wide monitoring of the emergence and spread of mutant K13 in Africa, and for studies into whether its emergence in Rwanda is a harbinger of subsequent partner drug resistance and ACT treatment failure.
evidence: Speculation based on data and knowledge of resistance evolution
